stem:
Solutions **F** and **G** each contain one cation and one anion. Eye protection was worn throughout.

| test | observations with **F** | observations with **G** |
|---|---|---|
| 1: aqueous sodium hydroxide, a few drops then in excess | grey-green precipitate; dissolves in excess to give a dark green solution | green precipitate, turning brown at the surface on standing; insoluble in excess |
| 2: aqueous ammonia, a few drops then in excess | grey-green precipitate; insoluble in excess | see part (d) |
| 3: dilute nitric acid, then aqueous silver nitrate | white precipitate | no change |
| 4: dilute nitric acid, then aqueous barium nitrate | no change | white precipitate |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Identify the cation in **F**.

options.rationale: Correct: grey-green hydroxide, soluble in excess NaOH but not in excess NH₃.
Fe(OH)₂ is green and does not dissolve in excess NaOH.
Zn(OH)₂ is white and dissolves in excess of both reagents.
Cu(OH)₂ is pale blue.

parts.explanation: Cr³⁺: Cr(OH)₃ is grey-green and amphoteric, forming dark green [Cr(OH)₆]³⁻.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Give the formula of the anion in **F**. (Type it as, for example, NO3-.)

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Write the ionic equation, with state symbols, for the reaction in test 3 with **F**. (Type it as, for example, Ba2+(aq) + SO42-(aq) -> BaSO4(s).)

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Predict the observations when aqueous ammonia is added to **G**, a few drops then in excess.

payload.template: A {{blank:a}} precipitate forms, which is {{blank:b}} in excess ammonia.

parts.explanation: Fe²⁺ gives green Fe(OH)₂ with ammonia, insoluble in excess (turning brown at the surface).

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Which reagent, used in excess, would distinguish a solution of Cr³⁺ from a solution of Zn²⁺?

options.rationale: Neither ion gives a visible change with dilute nitric acid.
Correct: Zn(OH)₂ dissolves in excess NH₃; Cr(OH)₃ does not.
This tests for sulfate, not the cation.
This tests for halide ions.

parts.explanation: Both hydroxides dissolve in excess NaOH (Cr: dark green, Zn: colourless), but only zinc dissolves in excess ammonia.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Give the formula of the anion in **G**.
parts.explanation: White precipitate with barium ions in acid: sulfate.

parts.label: (g)
parts.stem: State the cation in **G** and give the deductions that follow from the observations in test 1, including the change at the surface.

points.description: Green precipitate insoluble in excess NaOH is Fe(OH)₂, not amphoteric
Turning brown at the surface: oxidation by air (oxygen) of iron(II) hydroxide to iron(III) hydroxide, Fe(OH)₃

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: G contains iron(II) ions. The green precipitate, insoluble in excess, is iron(II) hydroxide, Fe(OH)₂, which is not amphoteric. At the surface, oxygen from the air oxidises iron(II) hydroxide to red-brown iron(III) hydroxide, so the precipitate browns.

parts.label: (h)
parts.stem: A freshly made dilute solution containing [Cr(H₂O)₆]³⁺ ions is violet, but in excess sodium hydroxide chromium(III) gives a dark green solution. Explain why the colour changes.

points.description: Ligand exchange: water ligands are replaced by hydroxide, forming [Cr(OH)₆]³⁻
The new ligands split the 3d orbitals by a different energy gap ΔE
So a different frequency (wavelength) of visible light is absorbed, and the complementary colour seen changes

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: In excess hydroxide the aqua ligands are replaced: Cr(OH)₃ + 3OH⁻ → [Cr(OH)₆]³⁻. Hydroxide ligands split the chromium(III) 3d orbitals by a different amount, ΔE, from water, so the d-d transition absorbs visible light of a different frequency and the complementary colour seen changes to dark green.

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: Give the oxidation state of chromium in the dark green complex formed in test 1.

parts.label: (j)
parts.stem: The precipitate formed by **F** with aqueous ammonia is chromium(III) hydroxide.
parts.explanation: True: Cr(OH)₃, grey-green, insoluble in excess ammonia.

explanation: F is chromium(III) chloride; G is iron(II) sulfate.
hints: Compare the behaviour of each precipitate in excess NaOH and in excess NH₃.
Silver halides identify halide ions; barium ions identify sulfate.

stem:
Solid **H** is a dark-coloured copper salt that dissolves in water to give a green-blue solution. Solution **J** contains one cation. Eye protection was worn.

| test | observations |
|---|---|
| 1: aqueous ammonia added to a solution of **H**, a few drops then in excess | pale blue precipitate; dissolves in excess to give a deep blue solution |
| 2: dilute nitric acid, then aqueous silver nitrate added to a solution of **H**; then dilute aqueous ammonia | cream precipitate; only partly dissolves in dilute ammonia |
| 3: aqueous sodium hydroxide added to **J**, a few drops then in excess | off-white precipitate, rapidly turning brown in air; insoluble in excess |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Give the formula of the cation in **H**.
parts.explanation: Pale blue hydroxide dissolving to deep blue in excess ammonia: Cu²⁺.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Identify the anion in **H**.

options.rationale: AgCl is white and dissolves in dilute ammonia.
AgI is yellow and insoluble even in concentrated ammonia.
Silver sulfate would not precipitate in dilute solution; sulfate is tested with Ba²⁺.
Correct: cream AgBr, partly soluble in dilute ammonia (soluble in concentrated).

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Write the ionic equation for the formation of the pale blue precipitate in test 1. (Type it as, for example, Fe2+ + 2OH- -> Fe(OH)2.)

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain the formation of the deep blue solution in test 1. Include the formula of the complex.

points.description: Ammonia molecules act as ligands (lone pair on N forms dative bonds to Cu²⁺)
A different ligand changes the splitting of the d orbitals (ΔE), so a different frequency of light is absorbed: deep blue

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: In excess, ammonia acts as a ligand, its nitrogen lone pair forming dative bonds to Cu²⁺. Four ammonia molecules replace four water ligands, giving the soluble complex [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺. Ammonia splits the d orbitals by a larger ΔE than water, so a different frequency of light is absorbed and the solution is deep blue.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Predict the observations when aqueous ammonia is added to **J**, a few drops then in excess.

payload.template: An {{blank:a}} precipitate forms, which {{blank:b}} on standing in air and is {{blank:c}} in excess ammonia.

parts.explanation: Mn²⁺: off-white Mn(OH)₂, rapidly turning brown in air, insoluble in excess.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Give the formula of the off-white precipitate formed in test 3.

parts.label: (g)
parts.stem: Why does the precipitate from **J** turn brown?

options.content: The precipitate loses water and becomes MnO.
options.rationale: MnO is not brown, and no heating occurs.

options.content: Carbon dioxide from the air forms manganese carbonate.
options.rationale: The colour change is oxidation, not carbonate formation.

options.content: Manganese(II) is oxidised by oxygen in the air.
options.rationale: Correct: higher oxidation state manganese oxides/hydroxides are brown.

options.content: Excess hydroxide forms a brown complex ion in solution.
options.rationale: The precipitate is insoluble in excess; the change is at the solid surface.

parts.explanation: Air oxidises Mn(OH)₂ to brown manganese(III)/(IV) oxides.

parts.label: (h)
parts.stem: Which reagent would distinguish a bromide from an iodide after adding silver nitrate?

options.rationale: Both precipitates are insoluble in dilute nitric acid.
This tests for sulfate.
Correct: AgBr dissolves; AgI does not.
This tests cations.

parts.explanation: Solubility of silver halides in ammonia: AgCl (dilute) > AgBr (concentrated) > AgI (insoluble).

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: Give the coordination number of copper in the deep blue complex.
parts.explanation: Four NH₃ and two H₂O ligands: 6.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Four NH₃ and two H₂O ligands: 6.

parts.label: (j)
parts.stem: State the identity of the cation in **J** and explain why the observations in test 3 rule out Fe²⁺ and Zn²⁺.

points.description: Fe²⁺ would give a green precipitate (not off-white); Zn²⁺ would give a white precipitate that dissolves in excess NaOH and does not turn brown

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: J contains Mn²⁺. Fe²⁺ would give a green precipitate rather than an off-white one, and Zn²⁺ would give a white precipitate that dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide and does not darken in air.

explanation: H is copper(II) bromide; J contains manganese(II).
hints: Use the colour of the silver halide and its solubility in ammonia.
Which hydroxide is off-white and darkens in air?
